extracted.intended_audience: courtiers, gentlemen, and readers seeking guidance on courtly conversation and witticisms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing and delivering pleasantries, repartee, and witty remarks appropriate to courtly/social occasions, including types of witticisms, tasteful limits, and rhetorical techniques illustrated by examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: playing_on_words
rubrics_metrics.description: This consists in changing a word by either adding or omitting a letter or a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: twisting a name or title (e.g., writing 'To my lady Emilia Impia' as a pun). Use small orthographic or phonetic changes to produce a humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: quoting_and_repurposing_verses
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote a verse or two, applying it to a purpose different from that which the author intends, or use a familiar saw sometimes to the same purpose but changing some word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: applying classical lines in unexpected contemporary contexts; altering a word in a known quotation to produce a witty retort (e.g., the Furiarum / Pascua example).

rubrics_metrics.name: interpret_names_and_onomastic_puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret names or pretend some reason why a man bears a particular name or why something is done, using etymological or language-based puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: joking that 'caglio' (Spanish) means 'I keep silence' to rebuke a babbler; offering double-meaning 'offices' (ufficio grande / ufficio della Madonna). Use knowledge of languages or sounds for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_same_word_in_different_sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a word that is familiar but use it in a sense different from the usual one to create wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: telling a trumpeter 'Cross over' and having him reply 'After your Lordship' using a different sense of 'passa'/'passi'. Exploit homonyms, polysemy, and context shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: take_words_but_not_sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the speaker's words literally but not his intended sense, replying to the literal utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: answering a Latin blessing with a punning Latin retort; replying in an unexpected language to taunt. This can produce a short, sharp laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: antithesis_and_balanced_contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Set words in opposition; contrasting clauses balanced against one another produce much grace and often wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'When will you cease throwing away your riches?' — 'When you cease stealing other men's.' Use structured parallels for elegance and bite.

rubrics_metrics.name: admit_and_reinterpret_another_speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm or admit what another speaker says but interpret it in a manner different from what was intended (turning praise or statement into a witty twist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: praising a lady and then reframing her age as resemblance to angels. Useful both for praise and a gentle rebuke; effective when accompanied by fine narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: preserve_and_extend_interlocutor_metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: When replying, preserve the same metaphor used by the interlocutor and extend or invert it for repartee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Palla degli Strozzi's 'the hen is hatching' leading to reply about hens not hatching away from nests. Keeps exchange cohesive and clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_metaphor_for_praise_or_taunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-arranged metaphors, especially as repartee, are effective for both praise and taunting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing a man to a false ducat placed among good ones to make him seem better; comparing warriors to money. Metaphors should fit the speaker's dignity and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_impiety_and_blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid impiety in witticisms: little reverence to God as an attempt at pleasantry is blameworthy and can lead to social exile or punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction: do not employ blasphemy or jokes that show irreverence toward God. This is a moral/social boundary not to be crossed.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_indecency_and_foul_speech_in_presence_of_ladies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid indecent, foul, or vulgar speech, and any witticisms intended to make ladies blush; show respect for women's presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a clever retort may be inappropriate if it becomes indecent in front of ladies (the Florentine/Sienese retort became unseemly). Consider audience composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: consider_time_place_persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Before using comparative similes or coarse comparisons, consider the time, place, persons, and other contextual factors repeatedly emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some liken people to animals or objects; such comparisons can be good or flat depending on context. Audience sensitivity and occasion matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: overstatement_and_understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyperbole (overstatement) or understatement to say things that outrageously exceed (or fall short of) the probable for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: describing someone as stooping to avoid hitting St. Peter's architrave; describing a servant carried up the chimney by smoke. Exaggeration creates surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: innuendo_and_tacit_implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use innuendo: say one thing while tacitly implying another, but avoid saying things that are obviously the complete opposite of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make absurd oppositions (calling a dwarf 'gigantic') except where the contrast itself is the joke; innuendo should be subtle. Example: saying someone might become a cardinal as a way of implying his rascality.

rubrics_metrics.name: ironic_dignified_taunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony that is dignified and sharp is becoming to great men and suitable in both jocose and serious matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King Alfonso's quiet, cutting comment about rings to the servant; use of polite phraseology to sting. Maintain composure and dignity when deploying irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: describe_evil_in_polite_terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe an evil or awkward thing using polite or euphemistic language to sting the subject indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: praising a pompous soldier by saying 'Saint Elmo has appeared' to indicate the danger is past; polite phrasing can be barbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: pretend_not_to_understand_dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A discreet man may pretend not to understand something that he does understand in order to produce a sharp or humorous effect (spicy dissimulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Marquess Federico's handling of the man with the hanged dove; Scipio's 'I am not at home' reply to Ennius. Feigned ignorance can turn the tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: retort_at_same_place_struck
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike back in the very same place where the interlocutor first struck — respond to the same angle or point for maximum effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quick repartees that mirror the original jab (Alonso Carillo's reply about being asked to be husband to save him from hanging). Mirroring increases sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: slow_gravity_and_patience_in_delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witticisms need an air of patience and are slowly uttered with a certain gravity, the delayed timing increasing their effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rustic jostling Cato and 'Have a care' — measured pacing and gravity can make a concise line funnier.

rubrics_metrics.name: explain_or_interpret_jocosely
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain or interpret things jocularly — offer a playful reinterpretation of an object, name, or situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calling the beautiful wife 'dama' and ugly husband 'asco/monster' as a play on words; light-hearted reinterpretation can amuse without malice.
